topic: The Cold War (1947–1991) was a rivalry between the United States and its allies and the Soviet Union and its allies, fought without direct war between them.
It was a struggle between capitalist democracy and communist one-party rule, waged through alliances, arms and space races, espionage, propaganda and proxy wars.
Its crises (Berlin, Korea, Cuba, Vietnam, Afghanistan) alternated with periods of détente.
It ended when the communist regimes of Eastern Europe fell in 1989 and the Soviet Union dissolved in 1991.

Terminology: George Orwell used 'cold war' in 1945 for a permanent standoff between nuclear powers.
Bernard Baruch and the journalist Walter Lippmann popularised it in 1947 for the US–Soviet rivalry.
Background: Distrust between the Western Allies and the Soviet Union predated the war and was only papered over during it.
At Yalta (February 1945) the Allies planned post-war Europe; Roosevelt's death and the atomic bomb changed the balance.
Iron Curtain, Iran, Turkey, Greece, and: Kennan's 'Long Telegram' (1946) and his 'X Article' argued that Soviet expansion should be contained.
Churchill warned of an 'Iron Curtain' across Europe; Soviet pressure on Iran and Turkey and the Greek Civil War raised tensions.
The Truman Doctrine (1947) promised US support to countries resisting communism: the policy of containment.
Marshall Plan, Czechoslovak coup and for: The Marshall Plan (1948) poured US aid into rebuilding Western Europe; the Soviets made their satellites refuse it.
Communists took full power in Czechoslovakia in 1948.
In 1949 Germany split into West Germany (Federal Republic) and East Germany (German Democratic Republic).
Espionage: Both sides spied intensively; Soviet agents had penetrated the Manhattan Project and the British establishment (Kim Philby).
Signals intelligence, spy planes and later satellites became central tools.
Cominform and the Tito–Stalin Split: Stalin created the Cominform (1947) to keep communist parties in line.
Yugoslavia's Tito refused to obey and was expelled in 1948, the first split in the Soviet bloc.
Berlin Blockade: In 1948 the Soviets cut land access to West Berlin to stop the new West German currency.
The Western Allies supplied the city by air for almost a year (the Berlin Airlift) until the blockade was lifted in 1949.
Beginnings of NATO and Radio Free Europe: The North Atlantic Treaty (1949) bound the US, Canada and Western European states to defend one another: NATO.
Western radio stations such as Radio Free Europe and Voice of America broadcast into the Eastern Bloc.
German rearmament: Chancellor Konrad Adenauer tied West Germany to the West; it rearmed and joined NATO in 1955.
The Soviet bloc answered with the Warsaw Pact the same year.
Chinese Civil War, SEATO, and NSC 68: Mao's Communists won China in 1949, the same year the Soviet Union tested its first atomic bomb.
The US document NSC 68 called for a massive military build-up; the US built alliances around the world (ANZUS, SEATO).
Korean War: North Korea, backed by Stalin, invaded the South in 1950; a US-led UN force pushed north until China intervened.
The war ended in stalemate and an armistice in 1953 near the original border, leaving Korea divided.
Nuclear arms race and escalation (1953–1: After Stalin's death (1953) both sides built hydrogen bombs and missiles; Sputnik (1957) started the Space Race.
The CIA backed coups in Iran (1953) and Guatemala (1954); the Soviets crushed the Hungarian Revolution (1956).
Castro's revolution (1959) made Cuba communist; the US-backed Bay of Pigs invasion failed (1961) and the Berlin Wall went up the same year.
From confrontation to détente (1962–1979: The Cuban Missile Crisis (1962) brought the world closest to nuclear war, and led to a hotline and a test-ban treaty.
The US fought a long, losing war in Vietnam; the Soviets crushed the Prague Spring (1968) under the Brezhnev Doctrine.
The Sino-Soviet split let Nixon open relations with China; détente produced the SALT arms treaties and the Helsinki Accords (1975).
Renewal of tensions (1979–1985): The Soviet invasion of Afghanistan (1979) ended détente; the US armed the Afghan resistance and boycotted the 1980 Moscow Olympics.
Reagan's arms build-up and the Strategic Defense Initiative raised tensions, while Solidarity challenged communist rule in Poland.
The Soviet economy stagnated under Brezhnev and his short-lived successors.
Final years (1985–1991): Mikhail Gorbachev launched reform (perestroika) and openness (glasnost) and sought arms deals, including the INF Treaty (1987).
In 1989 the communist regimes of Eastern Europe fell one after another and the Berlin Wall opened; Germany reunified in 1990.
After a failed hard-line coup in August 1991, the Soviet Union dissolved in December 1991.
Aftermath: Fifteen independent states replaced the USSR; Yugoslavia broke up in war.
Renewed rivalry between Russia and the West since the 2000s is sometimes called a 'Second Cold War'.
Influence: The United States emerged as the sole superpower in a unipolar world.
The Cold War shaped borders, alliances, technology and the global spread of capitalism.
In popular culture: Spy novels and films, nuclear-war fiction and Cold War-era themes remain staples of popular culture.
